items.body: Depeche Mode recorded their second album as a three-piece, and it is the only one in their catalogue made that way. Mute Records issued “A Broken Frame” on 27 September 1982, with Sire handling the United States. The English synth-pop band from Basildon, Essex, had lost founding songwriter Vince Clarke the previous December. The record turns 44 this year. Clarke left after the “Speak & Spell” tour finished in early December 1981 and formed Yazoo with Alison Moyet. Martin Gore took over the writing and wrote every track here. Alan Wilder had already answered a Melody Maker advertisement and played his first show with the band at Croc’s in Rayleigh, Essex, on 20 January 1982, but he was on a touring wage and did not play on the album. He became a full member in October 1982, the month after it came out. Gore addressed the arrangement in ZigZag No. 131 in November 1982, saying the band wanted the record to stand on its own before Wilder joined the studio line-up: “Alan started playing with us, but we wanted to make certain that any change in direction in our music wasn’t attributable to Alan joining. We needed to show we were capable of musical alteration by ourselves.” Wilder has given the other side of it: “I’d done my bit and I thought I warranted involvement. I had something to contribute. They said no.” Sessions ran from December 1981 to July 1982 at Blackwing Studios in London, where the room had moved up to a 16-track desk. Depeche Mode produced with Daniel Miller, and John Fryer and Eric Radcliffe engineered. Gore bought a PPG Wave 2 with his royalties and used it first on “See You”. Depeche Mode built the drums from an ARP 2600 for the bass drum and snares from a Roland TR-808 and a Korg KR-55. They also made their first attempt at sampling: Blancmange occupied the same building at the time and marched in front of microphones to supply the boots on “Shouldn’t Have Done That”. Miller described the change in method to Electronic Beats on 26 March 2013: “It was almost like a blank sheet of paper, the songs were recorded in a different way because Vince had a very specific idea of what the song was going to end up sounding like, and Martin didn’t really have that.” The ten tracks run 40 minutes and 52 seconds: “Leave in Silence”, “My Secret Garden”, “Monument”, “Nothing to Fear”, “See You”, “Satellite”, “The Meaning of Love”, “A Photograph of You”, “Shouldn’t Have Done That” and “The Sun & the Rainfall”. Dave Gahan sang lead throughout except on “Shouldn’t Have Done That”, a duet with Gore, and “Nothing to Fear” is an instrumental. The American edition used the longer 12-inch version of “Leave in Silence” and added a second instrumental, “Further Excerpts From: My Secret Garden”, making eleven tracks. Mute had put out three singles ahead of the album: “See You” on 29 January 1982, “The Meaning of Love” on 26 April 1982 and “Leave in Silence” on 16 August 1982, reaching numbers 6, 12 and 20 on the UK singles chart. The album reached number 8 on the UK albums chart, topped the UK independent albums chart, peaked at 22 in Sweden, 43 in New Zealand and 56 in Germany, and stalled at 177 on the Billboard 200. The BPI certified it gold on 30 August 1983. Brian Griffin photographed the sleeve, having also shot “Speak & Spell” and the band’s press images. Griffin cited Soviet socialist realism, Kazimir Malevich in particular, and German Romanticism as his references. Martyn Atkins designed the sleeve and Ching Ching Lee supplied the calligraphy. The band agreed to stay off the front cover; a solo picture of Andy Fletcher appeared on the back of the first pressing. In 1990 Life magazine placed the photograph on its list of the World’s Best Photographs 1980-1990. Reviews at the time were mixed. Steve Sutherland, writing in Melody Maker on 25 September 1982, called the album “ambitious and bold” while judging the band “essentially vacuous”. Smash Hits gave it 8 out of 10 in its 30 September to 13 October 1982 issue, with Peter Silverton writing that it showed “a lack of purpose”. Depeche Mode have been harder on it since. Gore told NME on 17 February 1990 that “musically A Broken Frame was a mish-mash”, and in a 2006 interview called it “probably our worst album”. Miller has kept a different line, describing it as “a transitional record and while it’s not their best record, it’s hugely important in terms of how it was made and how it gave everybody confidence.” Greek synth-pop duo Marsheaux recorded the album in full for Undo Records in 2015, later expanded to a 2CD with 12 bonus tracks. About Depeche Mode Vince Clarke, Martin Gore, Dave Gahan and Andy Fletcher formed Depeche Mode in Basildon, Essex, in 1980, taking the name from a French fashion magazine. Daniel Miller signed them to his independent label Mute Records and the synth-pop debut “Speak & Spell” followed in 1981, with Clarke writing most of it. His departure that December left Gore as the band’s writer for everything after it. “A Broken Frame” was the result, and the tour behind it ran through the UK and Europe with Wilder on stage from the start. He joined the studio line-up for “Construction Time Again” in 1983, the album on which Gareth Jones and sampled industrial sounds entered the band’s productions, as covered in Depeche Mode’s ‘Construction Time Again’. The Berlin sessions that followed produced “Some Great Reward” in 1984, then “Black Celebration” in 1986, “Music for the Masses” in 1987 and “Violator” in 1990, which carried “Personal Jesus” and “Enjoy the Silence”. Wilder left in 1995, after “Songs of Faith and Devotion” and the tour that followed it. The remaining trio issued “Ultra” in 1997, “Exciter” in 2001, “Playing the Angel” in 2005, “Sounds of the Universe” in 2009, “Delta Machine” in 2013 and “Spirit” in 2017. Fletcher died in May 2022. Gahan and Gore continued as a duo, releasing “Memento Mori” in 2023 and touring it, with the Mexico City shows becoming the concert film “M”. Forty-four years after Mute pressed it, “A Broken Frame” remains the record made in the gap between the two writers who shaped the band.

items.body: Da Punch is the fourth album from the Parisian project Krystal System. ‘Bonnie’ and ‘N°7’ are joined by a new member, bassist ‘Phi’, who had already appeared on the EP preceding the album. Remarkably, this is their first full-length release since 2013. On ‘Da Punch’, Krystal System takes a critical look at society and interpersonal relationships, resulting in a collection of 13 tracks. I’ve always had a soft spot for Krystal System because, to me, they sound like a big ‘f*** you’ to all those bands that simply keep repeating themselves, gradually getting lost in a lack of creativity. Krystal System continues along its established path, delivering uncompromising compositions that blend guitar and electronics into an Electro-Post-Punk sound, driven by Bonnie’s passionate vocals. She sometimes sings in her native French, but most of the tracks are performed in English, delivered with that unmistakable and rather sexy French accent. N°7 also takes the microphone, providing a nice counterbalance to the female vocals and occasionally resulting in a duet. The songs are varied and, as mentioned, uncompromising. Their cover of Front 242’s “Headhunter” is a great example. Rather than simply copying the original—which would be sacrilege—they give it their own interpretation, and it really works. There are other, even stronger tracks to discover, with Krystal System occasionally channelling Rammstein-like guitar riffs and Depeche Mode-style melodies, while still remaining firmly rooted in their own sound. That’s what I call a modern Punk attitude, and it really appeals to me. Krystal System will need to put themselves back on the map for a wider audience, but music lovers who already know the band will simply be delighted to see them return with such a cool album. (Rating:8). Listen to “A World That Is Yours”: A World That Is Yours by Krystal System About Krystal System Krystal System started in Paris, France, in April 2006 under the name Krystal. The founding duo was Bonnie on vocals and guitar and N°7 (also stylized as Seven) on vocals, synths, and programming. A first demo, “Demain n’existe pas,” came before the project gained early exposure through the 2007 International Cravefest Video Awards and concerts in France and Switzerland. Around 2007 the duo signed to Belgian label Alfa Matrix and adopted the name Krystal System. Their debut album, “Underground,” followed on November 14, 2008, then the seven-track EP “Underground: VooDoo Night Sessions” on November 27, 2009, “Nuclear” on June 17, 2011, and “Rage” on March 15, 2013. Krystal System returned in 2025 with the “Éclats Rouges” EP, its first studio release since “Rage” and its first with bassist φ (Phi), expanding the lineup to a trio. “Da Punch,” the fourth Krystal System album, followed on June 26, 2026, again with the trio of Bonnie, N°7, and Phi. The 13-track release was made available digitally via Bandcamp and on CD through the Alfa Matrix Store, whose edition adds two bonus tracks, “Newclear Winter” and a 2025 version of the track. The album also includes a cover of a Front 242 song, “Headhunter.”

items.album: ロバート・K・マートン
items.excerpt: ロバート・キング・マートンは1910年7月4日、米フィラデルフィアのスラム街でユダヤ系移民の子として生まれ、2003年2月23日にニューヨークで死去した、20世紀を代表するアメリカの社会学者です。出生名はマイヤー・ロバート・シュコルニック（Meyer Robert Schkolnick）。少年時代は手品師として活動しており、その芸名として一度「マーリン」を名乗り、後に「マートン」に落ち着いたという逸話が知られています。テンプル大学で社会学に触れ、ハーバード大学でピティリム・ソローキンやタルコット・パーソンズに師事して博士号を取得。ハーバード講師、チュレーン大学教授を経て、1941年にコロンビア大学に移り、以後ほぼ半世紀にわたって同大学を拠点としました（1979年に退官、名誉教授）。ポール・ラザースフェルドとともにコロンビア大学「応用社会調査研究所」を率いたことでも有名です。1957年にアメリカ社会学会（ASA）第47代会長を務め、1994年には社会学者として初めて全米科学賞（National Medal of Science）を受賞しています。続きをみる

items.excerpt: ジグムント・バウマン（Zygmunt Bauman、1925年11月19日〜2017年1月9日）は、ポーランド出身の社会学者・哲学者。「立法者と解釈者」、「造園管理人と猟場番人」、「固定化と液状化」といったメタファーを巧みに用いて今日のポストモダン社会の考察を深めるマルチ・リンガルの知識人として知られる。イギリス・リーズ大学、ワルシャワ大学の名誉教授であり、1971年からイギリスに定住し、ロンドン・スクール・オブ・エコノミクスで学んだのちリーズ大学の社会学教授、のちに名誉教授となった。続きをみる

items.excerpt: ハロルド・ガーフィンケル(Harold Garfinkel, 1917年10月29日-2011年4月21日)は、アメリカの社会学者で、「エスノメソドロジー」という社会学の一潮流を創始した人物です。カリフォルニア大学ロサンゼルス校(UCLA)で長く教鞭を執り、1967年に刊行した主著『Studies in Ethnomethodology(エスノメソドロジー研究)』によって、20世紀後半の社会学に独自の方法論的転回をもたらしました。20世紀に一つの主要な社会学的研究プログラムを打ち立てた数少ない社会学者の一人ともいわれています。続きをみる

items.album: タルコット・パーソンズ
items.excerpt: タルコット・パーソンズ(Talcott Parsons、1902年12月13日‐1979年5月8日)は、20世紀アメリカを代表する社会学者で、社会的行為の理論(action theory)と構造機能主義の確立者として知られますアメリカの古典的社会学の伝統に連なる人物で、社会的行為理論と構造機能主義で最もよく知られ、20世紀の社会学における最も影響力のある人物の一人とされています。1927年から1973年までハーバード大学で教鞭を執り、1930年に新設されたハーバード社会学部の最初期のメンバーとなり、後にはハーバード社会関係学部(Department of Social Relations)の設立にも中心的役割を果たしました1927年から1973年までハーバード大学の教員を務め、1930年には新設された社会学部の最初期の教員の一人となり、後にはハーバード社会関係学部の設立に尽力しました。続きをみる

items.album: ルネ・ジラール
items.excerpt: ルネ・ジラール(René Girard, 1923-2015)は、フランス生まれでアメリカを拠点に活動した文芸批評家・人類学者・思想家である。専門分野を横断しながら「人間の欲望は模倣的である」という一つの洞察を核に、文学、人類学、宗教学、心理学、経済学、政治哲学にまたがる巨大な理論体系を築き上げた。生前は「人文科学のダーウィン」と評され(哲学者ミシェル・セールの言葉として知られる)、没後もその影響力は衰えるどころか、シリコンバレーの起業家たちや現代の社会理論家たちの間でむしろ再評価が進んでいる人物である。続きをみる

items.body: DUKE ELLINGTON & JOHN COLTRANE - s/t (Impulse!, 1963) By Ferruccio Martinotti Sunday morning. We weren't even looking through Trane’s records, we already had a clear plan for the centenary. Then we spotted it. Or rather, it was almost as if IT was looking at us. There it was, humble and elusive amidst some truly gigantic "neighbors": “Duke Ellington & John Coltrane”. When a title says it all. How long had it been since it last took a spin on the turntable? A long, long time. So, we not only dusted it off, rescuing it from obscurity and oblivion but also cast it as the star of our own humble contribution to the Coltrane forum’s tribute. A quick preamble. Our favorite Trane is the one who burned all his bridges behind and embarked on the Path of Spiritual Ascension alongside Alice, Pharoah, Garrison, and Ali: for us, THIS is John’s definitive group. Since we are certain that our colleagues will, as usual, handle albums like ‘Interstellar Space”, “Olatunji”, “Live in Japan” et al, with the utmost mastery, we opted for a record you won’t find on "100 all-time best" playlists or among the essential albums by either Duke or Trane, yet one that is nonetheless deeply compelling. First things first: when and how did this encounter (the only one, if we’re not mistaken) between two of the greatest musicians of all time take place? The date: September 26, 1962. The setting: Rudy Van Gelder’s Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, a place so legendary that, like Atlantis, one wonders if it ever truly existed. The mastermind: Bob Thiele, a producer at Impulse! The Maestri arrived at the meeting from different trajectories, not just in terms of age, but artistically as well. Duke, at 63, as the old king of the jungle, having already changed the course of music history in the 1920s and 30s, he wanted to show the "young lions" that the time to end up in the zoo hadn't arrived just yet. And judging by the extraordinary “Money Jungle”, recorded right some weeks earlier along with Max Roach and Charles Mingus, he had every right to feel that way. Trane, meanwhile, aged 35, was in a transitional phase. Leading one of jazz’s most sensational lineups ever (Jones, Garrison, Tyner), he had just released his first album for Impulse! in 1962, a record where modal structures were handled sublimely, yet he had not entirely cut ties with a more “mainstream” approach to his music (though, given the musical context, quotation marks are essential here!). It was as if, mid-journey, he had paused to catch his breath and look back one last time, before lighting the fuse and blowing everything wide open. The two arrived at the studio bringing their respective rhythm sections: Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones for Coltrane; Aaron Bell and Sam Woodyard from Ellington’s orchestra. To glimpse a moment of that historic occasion, we can turn to bassist John Lamb, who was present that day: “There was no music on that whole date. Nobody had a chart. We came in and we were standing there, waiting to see what would have happen. Trane would go and sit on the piano bench with Duke. They didn’t talk but Duke would be singing and Trane would go. Then, after they did that for a few minutes, they got up. Trane would go to his microphone, Duke would start playing and the rhythm section, we had to do for ourselves, you know. That’s it. He didn’t even tell you the key. He could communicate without words and Trane could hear it.” The eight-hour session yielded seven tracks: “In a Sentimental Mood”, “Take The Coltrane” and “Stevie” (two sketches composed right there in the studio), “Angelica” and “The Feeling of Jazz” by Ellington; Billy Strayhorn’s “My Little Brown Book”; and Coltrane’s “Big Nick,” a tribute to tenor saxophonist Big Nick Nicholas. At work here are two living legends who set out not to change history, but simply to experience, with mutual respect and admiration, the intimate joy of music. No overbearing displays, no pointless academic showing-off or gratuitous virtuosity. Pure Magic. Even Elvin Jones puts down the sticks of dynamite and picks up the brushes. It is a "Sunday Morning Record", relaxed, atmospheric, and straightforward, reminding us that in our constant search for the ultimate, mind-blowing thrill (which, by definition, is NEVER the last one), we often lose sight of the wonder of simplicity. This is the perfect album to set that right. Let us leave the final word on this experience to Trane: “I was really honored to have the opportunity of working with Duke. It was a wonderful experience. He has set standards I haven’t caught up with yet. I would have liked to have worked over all those numbers again, but I guess the performances wouldn’t have had the same spontaneity. And they mightn’t have been any better.” May the Journey be light for you, dear John. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Listening to Crude Walnut Taste, it is tempting to focus on Giorgi Koberidze‘s compositional rigour: the electroacoustic transformations, the dialogue with Western classical forms, the microscopic attention paid to the behaviour of sound. Those elements are certainly there, but they risk obscuring something equally important. This is a remarkably funny album. After all, the opening track, “Horsing Around”, gives the game away immediately. Crude Walnut Taste is not funny in the sense of parody or quotation, but in the pleasure it takes in constantly wrong-footing the listener who might be expecting an academic work. A gesture suddenly changes direction, a rhythmic idea gathers momentum before being interrupted by an entirely different line of thought. Titles such as “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio” and “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” gesture towards familiar classical forms, but only long enough for Koberidze to dismantle them. As the composer explains in the accompanying interview, these references belong to an earlier period of his practice, when his relationship with classical composition was more direct and, in his own words, more “primitive”. And this is the paradox at the heart of the album. On the one hand it sounds almost primitive, built from raw acoustic matter; on the other, the speed with which ideas appear, collide and disappear constantly propels it forward. Without resorting to the tired label of “retro-futurism”, the image that kept returning while I listened was Georgiy Daneliya’s Kin-dza-dza!. The 1986 Soviet science-fiction comedy follows two ordinary citizens transported to a distant galaxy where advanced civilisation appears to have regressed into something primitive. The film was, of course, scored by the late Georgian composer Giya Kancheli, yet there is a comparable measure of irony and lightness of touch running through both works. That playfulness extends to the sound world itself. Much of the album is constructed from recordings of the doli, the Georgian drum, chosen precisely because it carries no melodic baggage. Rather than treating the instrument as a symbol of national identity, Koberidze breaks it down into tiny fragments that become the raw material for an unexpectedly broad range of textures. The result is music that remains unmistakably physical. Even the electronics rarely transform those sounds outright. However, what remains most surprising, is the album’s speed, and not just its manic kinetic energy, but also the speed with which ideas appear only to mutate. Very little is allowed to settle. Musical thoughts collide with a kind of controlled frenzy that recalls someone thinking faster than they can speak. And yet, despite this restless surface, the music never feels erratic. It remains playful without becoming flippant, rigorous without turning solemn. That is a rare balance, and one that gives Crude Walnut Taste its distinctive character. To help us crack the walnut, we approached Giorgi Koberidze directly. Crude Walnut Taste began life as a 20-channel spatial work commissioned for MONOM’s 4D Sound system before being reimagined in stereo for this release. How did the process of translating such a physically immersive piece into a two-channel format affect your relationship to the material? Were there aspects of the original spatial architecture that had to be sacrificed, or did the reduction reveal new details that were previously hidden? I actually already knew how the piece would sound in stereo, because I don’t have a twenty-channel speaker setup at my studio. So while working on it, I was composing in stereo from the start, imagining what sound could fit where. We then spent two weeks at MONOM Studio in Berlin, where we had the chance to rearrange the piece, add things, and sometimes exclude things, but the core idea of the music was already written in stereo, and that’s what made it possible to translate the twenty-channel piece back down. Of course, a lot is lost in that reduction, but the core idea is still there. It works almost the same as watching an IMAX film in a normal movie theatre: whatever really matters stays in focus, stays at the centre. What the IMAX size gives you additionally is maybe more air, more space, something that isn’t crucial to understanding the film itself. I’d say it’s the same with this piece: what really matters is still there in stereo. The MONOM system just gives more space and some additional ideas, but I wouldn’t say the piece is focused only on those twenty channels. Generally, my belief is that good music can be played on a single-string guitar, even if it was written for a hundred-channel system, as long as the idea itself is strong, and as long as the music matters more than the form. If we’re not talking about a piece where form is more important than the music, then I think it’s easily translatable anywhere. Across Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, its Epilogue, and now Crude Walnut Taste, the doli seems to occupy an increasingly central role in your work. On this album, the instrument is extensively sampled, dissected and reconstructed through micro-editing techniques. What drew you to the doli as the primary sonic source, and how did transforming it electronically alter your perception of an instrument so deeply embedded in Georgian musical culture? I use the doli because it has no pitch. My problem with using tonal instruments from the Caucasus – the duduk, say, or the chuniri – is that they come with already-written melodies and harmonies, and I find it very hard to know how to use that material in modern music. At some point I decided I would never touch existing melody or harmony, because it’s already there, it’s already enough. It doesn’t need anything from me, or from anyone, to be transformed. The doli is interesting because you can use it without ever touching a melody or a harmony, it gives you a lot of possibility to take micro-material from it instead. But anyone who understands sound and sound design knows that, basically, you can turn any sound into anything. The instrument you choose is just a source for material, and from there you can go anywhere; it’s really about what physical material you’re comfortable working with. In my case, it’s the doli simply because it’s here – you’re in Georgia, there are dolis everywhere, you can just grab one. Also, the quality of that sound already carries something very familiar to every Georgian. By using it, you’re lightly touching this historical heritage, but it doesn’t give you licence to overuse it – to base your music on something already precious to Georgians and then claim it as your own. Some people use old melodies, traditional melodies especially, and I’m not against using old pop music in modern work. But when it comes to traditional music, it’s more delicate. So even when we do use tonal instruments like the duduk, we’re very careful never to cross into an already-written melody from Georgian folk music. Earlier works such as Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests felt almost cartographic, mapping landscapes, memories and imagined geographies through graphic scores, ensembles and field recordings. Crude Walnut Taste seems more focused on texture, gesture and acoustic matter itself. Do you see this album as a departure from those narrative and spatial concerns, or as another way of exploring the relationship between place, memory and sound? Also, several track titles—”Tbilisian Faux-Valse”, “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio”—appear to reference established musical forms, yet the music itself constantly undermines expectations through fragmentation, electroacoustic processing and playful subversion. To what extent are these titles intended as affectionate dialogues with classical traditions, and how important is humour or irony within your compositional practice? First, some context: Crude Walnut Taste was actually written much earlier than Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests – about five years earlier. What the two albums share is a certain playfulness with, and closeness to, classical music. In 2019, when I wrote Crude Walnut Taste, I was a much younger student of classical composition, so the way I integrated that knowledge into the album was more direct, less hidden, even a bit more “primitive” – the melodic and harmonic moments lean more overtly classical. That’s also where the track titles come from, which I actually chose later, closer to the album’s release: names like “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” or “Quasi Sonata-Allegro.” They’re not literal sonata-allegros or waltzes, of course, but the mood and the harmonic gestures really are drawn from there. Looking back, I wouldn’t use these references so directly today – in Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, similar techniques are used much more hidden, on a deeper, more background level. So, from that perspective, this earlier album carries a bit of irony, a bit of humour, and that’s something I’m quite fond of. I’ve always wanted to find a way to put humour inside music – it’s genuinely hard to do. My friend and musical collaborator Luka, the other half of Awwwaea, always used to come up with wonderfully funny musical ideas; I was constantly amazed at how he could make our whole friend group laugh for hours over a single musical idea. I’d say this album carries a little of that same spirit. At the same time, it’s a very personal record. Even the title comes from childhood: crude walnut taste refers to eating very raw, unripe walnuts as kids – cracking them open with your fingers while they’re still green, watching your fingers turn green and then black from the juice. That taste takes me straight back to those childhood memories: sometimes fast, sometimes a little sad, but mostly very bright, full of colourful images and imagination – but still raw, because the sounds themselves are raw. After I finished the album, a friend told me at a small concert that it felt like “music made for sounds no one else is using.” I loved that description, because the sounds you hear really are raw – almost taken straight from the computer as they are, with very little additional sound design or processing layered on top. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. A surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics Stars are Crashing, Home are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet by Fallen   Like a shield of emotive melodic strands gathering before our eyes, Lorenzo Bracaloni’s Fallen project shifts through time and space, blending ethereal voices with instrumental electronica across the long-winded (but apropo) Touched Music title, Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet. Fifteen slices of life unfold through ambient propulsion, opening with cascading sonic beauty on “Rusted Gardens,” where pitter-patter patterns breathe against a spacious atmosphere, quietly revealing how essential sound can be. Bracaloni’s signature drifts into darker territory with “Violent Winds,” yet remains light and airy, its floating voices drawing us deeper into a mesmerizing current. Downtempo bubbles and understated beatwork provide a gentle respite on “Wide Red Skies.” These are tranquil, ethereal spaces where music opens pathways rather than directing the listener. “The Vanishing,” “Hearts are Changing,” “Chasing Mechanical Butterflies,” and “From Dry Iron Valleys to Utopian Realms” could each have formed the core of a powerful extended player, while closing piece “Direction Home (Ruins Pathway)” ignites something deeper, allowing everything that came before to drift into one surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics, emotional textures, and shifting plateaus. Early heavyweight ambient/IDM artists such as Arovane, Biosphere, and Global Communication, alongside cinematic world-builders like Yagya, Secede, and Deepchord / Echospace, will find familiar connections throughout. As a result, Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet is available on Touched Music. items.body: Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage Distort Everything Forever by SUAHN   SUAHN is Michael York, Baltimore-based, and his music has been moving through bass music, acid, techno, jungle, and experimental club forms long enough that Distort Everything Forever doesn’t arrive sounding like a debut. York grew up hearing hand-me-down mix CDs from his uncle, Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares sitting next to The Cure and Bauhaus on the same tape. That detail explains a lot about the harsher edges of what he makes. Four Tet, RL Grime, Ivy Lab, and Boombox Cartel have all picked up his catalog. He appeared on VISION‘s MISSION 03 compilation alongside Billain, Posij, Current Value, and others. So the full-length context is already there before a single track plays. The opener “Reverie” starts in ambience. Gives the impression things might unfold slowly. That doesn’t last. Heavy bass, drum and bass breaks, distorted percussion, hip hop rhythmic ideas, it arrives fast and stays physical for most of the runtime. York doesn’t spend time introducing himself. The drums show up and the record commits. The title is a literal description of the production language. Distortion isn’t decoration here, it bleeds into everything. Drums, bass, breaks, vocal fragments, transitional material. At a certain point it stops being an effect and becomes the identity of the record. There’s drum and bass underneath a lot of this, but also half-time hip hop programming, bass music, and the heavier side of experimental club production. Points where it touches the same territory as VISION releases—beat-driven material where drum and bass structure gets slowed, stretched apart, and rebuilt around enormous low end. “Drifting” is where the album properly declares itself. Old school drum and bass instinct in the way it moves. Not especially melodic, doesn’t need to be. The drums do most of the talking. Filter sweeps and frequency movement pull you further in gradually, and York trusts the breaks to establish the personality of the track without constantly dropping another melodic idea on top. That restraint is what makes the track land. “Lost in it All” goes heavier. Half-time rhythms, bass with real dub-like weight, distortion threatening to tear it apart at the edges. This is where the VISION comparison becomes most useful, the heavier beat-focused side of NOISIA‘s label, where sound design carries as much importance as composition and a bass hit functions almost like a lead instrument. York understands that language. The saturation and distortion give his version a dirtier edge than most producers working in that space would allow. The tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to :: Worth noting what heavy distortion actually costs at the mix stage. Once you start saturating bass, drums, and midrange simultaneously, everything generates additional harmonics that compete for the same frequency space. Transients lose definition. Low mids turn to mud. The challenge is making something sound destroyed while still giving every important element enough room to be understood. York handles this well, the tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to, but the kicks still hit, the bass still has shape, and the breaks never collapse into an undefined wall of noise. That kind of control doesn’t happen accidentally. “How Dark it Gets” is another standout, specifically for the vocal work. Fragments getting chopped, repositioned, distorted, thrown against the breaks, the edits never become a gimmick because they function as another rhythmic layer. Small pieces surface, disappear, return processed differently. The track feels like it’s constantly rearranging itself while you’re inside it. What becomes clear across the full runtime is how studied York is in this corner of electronic music. The Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares references from his background make sense, but this isn’t an IDM record in the older Warp or Rephlex sense. The center of gravity is heavier, connected to modern bass production, jungle, drum and bass, industrial club music, and the post-NOISIA school of extremely controlled sound design. Someone who understands what happens when breaks become texture, when distortion becomes arrangement, when bass stops functioning as low end and starts carrying the emotional weight of a track. The sequencing does real work too. Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The quiet at the beginning and the quiet at the end aren’t the same quiet. Everything that happened between them changes what the stillness means. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage. That’s a complete thought. Distort Everything Forever is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Multiple active listens never feel like a chore, and are instantly rewarded by the lavishness of the sounds and the cleverness of the compositions, bringing together awe, humor, and bewilderment. And what else can we ask of experimental music? This aesthetic of contrast between composite lumps of sound and silence Der Saal tobt by Ervin Omsk   From Switched-On Bach to countless orchestral sound libraries promising to be hyper realistic, the history of electronic music’s mimicry of and liaison with classical spans over half a century. Most of the time, this relationship has manifested in two clear-cut ways: imitation and reinterpretation. A frequent intention is to make electronics act like the expansive (and expensive) organ of the orchestra or chamber ensemble, trying to sound as close as possible to the “real thing,” such as in a lot of pop music and soundtracks; but on the other (more intriguing) hand, electronic composers have also looked back at classical to reinterpret it through new technologies and sensibilities: the aforementioned 1968 study of baroque on the Moog synthesizer by Wendy Carlos, or Tomita’s Snowflakes Are Dancing (1974) performing the impressionistic romanticism of Debussy, all the way to recent takes on minimalism such as Erik Hall’s half-acoustic-half-electronic recreations or, to take it to the extreme and to a more underground angle, composermodel’s MF18M, an excellent all-midi, trance-infused rendition of Steve Reich‘s Music for 18 Musicians. A glaringly underrepresented style however is the manic use of the orchestra in works such as Luciano Berio’s 1969 Sinfonia, or Pierre Boulez’s Dérive 1 (1984), or what one might call the the final boss in this most-chaotic “genre,” Karleinz Stockhausen’s Gruppen (1955-57), for three orchestras (yes, three). Save for some pieces (like the title track), Ervin Omsk’s latest Der Saal tobt’(“The Hall in uproar”) is closer to these works than to, say, an extreme decomposition of club music. The opening track, “Memo Grisaille,” makes it instantly clear: isolated clusters of sound straddling between strings, brass, and pure electric glitches come and give way to silence, before they start interacting in a complex and wider tapestry of sounds. This aesthetic of contrast between composite lumps of sound and silence recurs throughout Der Saal tobt, and the whitespace makes each sonic assault all the more flavorful. Every pseudo-instrument is crafted to be as full and satisfying a sound as possible: in “Echt jetzt” (“seriously…?”) hyper-speed delays make each percussive atom resonate more like held notes than bells or beats. When actual long-held synths do appear, like in the following “Greller Block” or in “Offenes Feld” (“Garish Block” and “Open Field” – maybe opposites?) the drones still appear unstable, as if they were about to implode and, after a second of tension, explode back into shards of colour. Which happens in between tracks anyway. A simple industrial piece to a positively jarring experience :: Interestingly, the title track (and single) of the album is somewhat of a different affair. It is probably the only piece with a clear rhythm–if syncopated to excess–played by airy synths with tones bending sharply like glissandos rather than drum samples. This attention to original sound design turns the rhythm from what could have been a simple industrial piece to a positively jarring experience: why am I nodding along to this? How come my body recognizes the pace? This more rhythmic approach comes back in “Nicht senden doch senden” (“do not send send anyway”), mixed in with everything else, from the glitchy delays to the bent pitches, before the closer “Beim besten Willen” (“with the best will in the world”) harkens back to the opener and to XX century atonality with the full-on orchestral stirring bringing the record to a full circle. It’s hard to find any obvious point of comparison in contemporary electronic music, if not maybe some of Nathan Ho’s serialist work or Rashad Becker’s Traditional Music of Notional Species; but where Becker’s “Dances” and “Themes” sounded like linguistic attempts at communication from an alien civilisation, Ervin Omsk’s compositions are impressionistic and expressionistic, conveying a much more holistic content. While the first reaction to an album like this could very well be “how the hell was this made,” especially for someone who dabbles in making experimental music–the press release mentions manipulated recordings of an alto recorder and pure synthesis, but there just must be more!–something that distinguishes Der Saal tobt from a lot of technical or academic-leaning avant-garde electronics is its allure, and the persuasiveness with which it leads the listener further in. Multiple active listens never feel like a chore, and are instantly rewarded by the lavishness of the sounds and the cleverness of the compositions, bringing together awe, humor, and bewilderment. And what else can we ask of experimental music? Der Saal tobt is available on Orange Milk. items.body: Everything about the sound design and palette of Window To Askoy seems suspended in the heat of summer rains and tropical smog. Yet it’s the soulful element that’s paramount: an exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss shape the ventricles and vessels of these lean cuts. Exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss Zoku – Zoku maintain the altitude of their own exciting frequencies alongside the heights and depths of the frankly awesome Strugatsky Brothers album Window To Askey. Atmosphere is the key ingredient here. There is beauty, tenderness and a sense of wisdom and maturity visible beneath an overt display of technique. The realms created are dub-heavy in tension and color, occasionally recalling Bvdub, but this isn’t intended as a direct comparison. The brothers (Stas Kovalev, aka Keiss) are clearly distinct, yet that fugue-like quality and deftness of hand is apparent throughout. Rain features, reverbs write verbs across low-hung bass, while beats staccato in and out of the visual field being created. Mid-range tension stutters into view only to evaporate moments later. Everything about the sound design and palette seems suspended in the heat of summer rains and tropical smog. Yet it’s the soulful element that’s paramount: an exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss shape the ventricles and vessels of these lean cuts. Across ten tracks and three extras, the brothers retain interest and keep expectations poised on the edge of what’s possible next, doing so with rare panache. I might call this ambient, but that would be a lazy get-out. This is experimental electronic music wearing its influences on clean sleeves, facing forward with valor, integrity and just enough—and plenty—of both. Recommended for the ethereal textured moods of FSOL and the abstract dub’n fuzz of Jack Dangers. Window To Askoy is available on Zoku – Zoku. items.body: All in all, an emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip, augmented by dark clouds of noisy elements. An emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip Lost Myths vol. VII by Lost Myths   Based in Achères, France, Lotophagus Records is an indie label with a real interest in unusual and captivating music, crossing the paths of radical experimentalism and various researches into sound morphologies and advanced or hand-crafted electronic manipulations. I discovered their catalogue a while ago and, to say the least, it is full of intriguing albums covering a large spectrum of electronic music sub-genres. I stopped on this new one first for the originality of the concept brought to the fore. The creative motivation of this album lies behind the discovery of a “born to fail” fantasist electro-acoustic instrumentarium with a curious, if not enigmatic, name: Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium. Without entering into the heavily technical description of this machinery, we can see associations with electro-physical instruments and utopian automatic music forged by acousticians and genuinely crazy inventors of the past, such as J. B. Schalkenbach. The Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium, as suggested by its etymology, seems to combine pseudoscience with metaphysical concerns about aetheric properties of sounds: in brief, a noise-producing machine capable of providing magical effects, surrounded by a surreal-futuristic dimension and appealing electroacoustic fairy-like undulating resonances. It is easy to imagine those charming and Dada-esque musical-technical inventions linked to the fruitful artistic creativity of the early 20th century, notably the challenging and humorous poetical universe of Picabia and, more precisely, the steampunk-before-its-time adventurous imaginary world of Albert Robida. Lost Myths is almost an anonymous and highly secret project, as is the Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium itself. The album starts with an awe-inspiring ghostly beauty built on altered choir sequences and fuzzed-out, almost static droney emotional phrases with a sense of depth, nostalgia, and rumbling darkness. The following tracks oscillate between chilling abstract electronica for bleak tones, hauntological effects, distorted micro-noises, and anomalous industrial-mechanical accidents. All in all, an emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip, augmented by dark clouds of noisy elements. Somewhere between the lo-fi sonic explorations of Modelbau, Pedestrian Deposit, and Cremation Anxiety. Lost Myths vol. VII is available on Lotophagus. [Bandcamp] Lost Myths vol. VII by Lost MythsThe post Lost Myths :: Lost Myths vol. VII (Lotophagus) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: The funk Isaac Hayes and Willie Hutch wrote for American crime films in the early 1970s has a second home in Hamburg, a city whose funk scene runs through The Mighty Mocambos, Bacao Rhythm & Steel Band and the Légère Recordings label. The Winston Brothers come straight out of that scene, and “Get On Down” opens their second album, Sweets, out on 6 November via Ohio’s Colemine Records. It starts at full tempo: a hard breakbeat, choppy guitar chanks and a two-man horn section. Multi-instrumentalist and producer Sebastian Nagel and drummer Lucas Kochbeck formed the band as a school project, and Nagel describes the partnership in one line: “It’s a family thing, and we really know each other well.” Both play in Bacao, Nagel has also played with the Mocambos, and Kochbeck with Hamburg Spinners, part of a circuit where the same players keep turning up in each other’s line-ups. Sweets draws on that circuit, with Kimo Eiserbeck on saxophone and flute, Hans Stephan on trumpet and Carsten Meyer, the Hamburg keyboardist known as Erobique, on synths. Extra drums come from Max Weissenfeldt, once of Munich’s The Poets of Rhythm and now working as Max Whitefield. Sax and trumpet stick to short, angular stabs, the punctuating role horns play on the Hayes and Hutch scores. Midway the band drop into a dub-style section with delay on the instrumental parts, and the drums carry on underneath: like Drift, their 2022 debut, the track is built on the break. Stream “Get On Down” HERE and order Sweets ahead of release through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: The Winston Brothers – Get On Down appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 989The British prog band Karnataka was formed in Swansea, Wales, in 1997. It's one of the leading names in British contemporary progressive rock, despite some intermittency. It was disbanded in 2004, reformed in 2005, suspended in 2017 and returned in 2023. Their sound is known for fusing classic progressive rock with influences from Celtic music, folk, and symphonic atmospheres, often standing out for powerful female vocals and accessible melodies. One of its founding members, Ian Jones, is the only remaining member in the band. The name "Karnataka" was chosen after Jones' trip to India. Karnataka released six studio works, "Karnataka" in 1998, "The Storm" in 2000, "Delicate Flame Of Desire" in 2003, "The Gathering Light" in 2010, "Secrets Of Angels" in 2015 and this one "Requiem For A Dream"."Requiem For A Dream" is Karnataka's most ambitious work to date. At almost 80 minutes long, it marks the band's return after an eight-year hiatus. Lirically, it's a concept album exploring personal adversity and global chaos. It strongly addresses the climate changes and the destruction of the planet. The lyrics balance the despair and loss with a persistent search for hope and a "new beginning" for all humanity. Musically, the album alternates between epic tracks with multiple variations in themes, tones and even modes, and more concise pieces. As a concept album, it's best enjoyed in one sitting and, despite its 79 minutes, it never becomes tedious. It presents a great luxurious production.So, "Requiem For A Dream" is the sixth studio album of Karnataka that was released in 2023. The line up on the album is Sertari (vocals, backing vocals and choir) and Ian Jones (bass guitar, bass pedal, keyboards, piano and acoustic guitar). "Requiem For A Dream" had also the participation of Luke Machin (guitars), Gonzalo Carrera (keyboards), Troy Donockley (uilleann pipes and low whistles) and Chris Allan (drums and percussion), all as guest musicians.The album begins and ends with the whispered words "tick-tock". "All Around The World" captures our attention with its subtle mood. It features a beautifully vocal line. The verses and chorus flow seamlessly into each other with a touch of levity and grace. It has stunning guitar solo work. It's one of its longest tracks. "Sacrifice" has a distinctive character. It allows you to lose yourself in a dreamlike state, swaying your senses with an ethereal sound that leaves an intimate aftertaste. Here, Sartori displays her wide variety of vocal skills. This is a luminous track with transparent orchestration. "Look To The East" combines a hit song with a touch of oriental harmonies. The vocals have a subtle radiance and lightness. It's a well-produced piece with some good vocal effects, sumptuous synths and programming. It has quite a commercial impact upon the ears. "Forgiven" is the second lengthy track. It's an illuminated fabulous ballad, polished and effective in every detail with a spiritual vibe surrounding it with its Latin chanting. It's elevated by an amazing vocal performance from Sartori. It's one of my favorite tracks on the album, a real great work that by itself is worth the album. "The Night's Dance" has a vaporous elegance that offers another triumphantly gorgeous melodic line. It's a lush track with a very beautiful melody, beautifully sung, alongside great orchestration. It's pretty straight ahead, but it does not need to be complicated, as Sertari is the star here. "Say Goodbye Tomorrow" is an up-tempo number with a great guitar work and synth touches in the middle. It's another breath of lightness in the form of a casual track. It's a hopeful and positive song, expressed forcefully via strong voice and a stunning chorus. "Don't Forget My Name" is another ballad, but with a melancholic touch. It's emotional, with tight playing, sensorial impact and meaningful music. Sertari shines amidst frantic guitar struts, pulsating drum rolls, and accompaniment buried deep in the background. The title track is the third longest, the lengthiest, a twenty-five-minute epic. During the running time of the piece, all those ingredients that make Karnataka a melodic prog institution are up front and centre. There are some heavy passages, but above all, there is some more of the pop/prog fusion the band have always done so well. And the orchestration is again well done. It seals, probably, the most mature production in the band's canon releases. This is another track likely to become an onstage favourite. So, to conclude, this is an amazing perfect ending to the album where the lengthy tracks are the best.Conclusion: "Requiem For A Dream" is another great album from this Welsh band. They have never disappointed me, and again they deliver another flawlessly work, indeed. Like a true craftsman, Jones has once again created a piece that deserves to be heard by all those for whom progressive rock is above all a source of pleasure and emotion. They are 80 minutes of melodic adventure of the very finest quality. All things that epitomise Karnataka are captured on this album: ambitious songs, great playing, intelligent lyrics, beautiful symphonic sounds, lovely female voice and fine guitar work. The attention to detail is staggering, which helps to keep things fresh with repeated listenings. This is a band and an album that deserves to be better known. Fans of progressive and symphonic music owe it to themselves to give it a go.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*

After contributing to the album *Palepolitana* by the veterans of Osanna in 2015, then reviving her former band Presence for a sixth studio album?the unclassifiable *Masters and Following*, an unlikely encounter between Keith Emerson's *Inferno* (1980) and Lacrimosa's *Inferno* (1995)?and before playing a major role in a seemingly endless (3 jam-packed CDs) tribute to Bowie/Bolan?which also featured Fran
items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Sophya Baccini is no stranger to the world of prog rock. After contributing to the album *Palepolitana* by the veterans of Osanna in 2015, then reviving her former band Presence for a sixth studio album?the unclassifiable *Masters and Following*, an unlikely encounter between Keith Emerson's *Inferno* (1980) and Lacrimosa's *Inferno* (1995)?and before playing a major role in a seemingly endless (3 jam-packed CDs) tribute to Bowie/Bolan?which also featured Franck Carducci?Sophya (originally named Sofia, then Sophia) gave us an update in 2023, both on stage (performing covers of classics by Yes and Kate Bush, for example) and in the studio with *Animatesi*, released in January?a more intimate album than usual, featuring Sophya alone at the piano. And in the second half of 2023, she's finally back with an album by Aradia, her all-female band equally possessed by the spirit of baroque progressive rock. Unlike *Big Red Dragon*, her previous album, *Runnin' with the Wolves* doesn't feature a lineup of prestigious guest artists. Sophya and her rousing piano are backed by a formidable all-female lineup: Marilena on keyboards, Francesca on violin, Sonia on guitar and saxophone, Anais on bass, and Chiara on drums?a rarity in the world of prog that's worth noting, especially since this testosterone-free lineup gives this baroque RPI an uncommon elegance. Nevertheless, we find here the signature style that Sophya has been developing for years, both as a solo artist and with Presence?a sort of decadent, theatrical rock that owes a great deal to the Bowie of the '70s, to Sparks (she even covered "This Town Ain't Big Enough for Both of Us" on Presence's latest album), to Kurt Weill and the most tender, romantic Kate Bush, without ever straying far from Italian symphonic prog in the vein of Banco. It's a curious combination that warrants a detailed description of the seven tracks that make up this intriguing *Runnin' with the Wolves*. More than once or twice, more than three or four times?let's say half a dozen times?I've tried to put into words what came to mind while listening to these melancholic waltzes, these sophisticated arrangements, these progressive lullabies, and the highly elaborate structure of the lengthy "Continua" (9:17), but it was a lost cause. I couldn't write without letting go of the brakes on my imagination without stumbling over every syllable. Because *Runnin' with the Wolves* is an album that can't be described but must be listened to endlesslyAt a time when Taylor Swift's sanitized, slightly WASP-ish pop sells millions of copies worldwide and racks up billions of views on YouTube?all while scrupulously adhering to the "rule of three": no more than three chords, no more than three notes in the melody, and no more than three beats in the rhythm (and often only two)?does music as genuinely warm and colorful as Sophya Baccini's have a place in this grand burlesque spectacle that means so much to all of us: modern music? Yes, but only a small spot at the very back of the room, perhaps insufficiently but proudly illuminated by media outlets like this one. So let's shine a light on it?let's be enlightening and enlightened?in the hope of encouraging as many people as possible to listen closely to this entirely female, one-of-a-kind prog band.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — The passage of 30 years and a (duh, this is Polish neo prog after all) different vocalist notwithstanding, this reminds me of COLLAGE's classic "Moonshine" album, the one that still dwarfs most of the British giants. The problem is, it recalls the excesses of that masterpiece rather than its massive triumphs that inspired so much more from that country and beyond. Apparently conceived to lighten the mood amongst the lyrically downbeat sentiments of the reunion album "Over and Out" and to accompany it on the tour, "One and Only" should have been patterned after the sumptuous "Living in the Moonlight" rather than the bloated "In Your Eyes", which indeed means it's pretty good for the first half and abysmal for the home stretch. In the end, for a presumably lighter number, it's one of their most oppressive songs and I'd rather bathe in the tears of "What about the Pain (a family album)" a thousand times before I hear this again.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Kimmo P'RSTI's fourth album is a symphonic folk-prog-country affair featuring inspiring guest appearances, an analog sound, and Kimmo battling AI. His style ranges from Genesis and Yes to Supertramp, Camel, and Caravan."Circle of Wagons" showcases a distinctive folk-prog universe, a medieval touch in neo-classical mode, and a solemn sound reminiscent of Camel'it's a given. The choir, the melody that evokes Unitopia, the Archangel, and the cinematic drift on the famous "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" are all present. The guitar solo adds a touch of nostalgia to the repetitive melody, and the outro flute hints at the arrival of the alien. "Carousel" features fruity guitar, swirling keyboards, and a vintage instrumental that flirts with the "dinosaur" aesthetic, a tribute to JP Boffo. "Nightmares Come to Consume" features a fruity and catchy saxophone riff, reminiscent of PANZERPAPPA, but with a touch more Phil COLLINS. The shunt is a highlight, while the chorus becomes repetitive. "Chasing Echoes" has an airy, western-tinged melancholy feel, with a melting intro that perfectly captures the current mood. The vintage organ amplifies the effect of this beautiful, plaintive ballad, with vocals provided by one of the four regular members on this otherwise conventional track. "Things Not Seen" has the sound of a CAMEL album; Risto's saxophone brightens the air, the symphonic keyboard drift flirts with TANGERINE DREAM, followed by a blazing guitar solo and a prominent bassline that grabs your attention. The track is a versatile, danceable pop gem."In My Life" follows in the same vein, with a guitar solo and a raspy vocal that amplify the depth of this AMBROSIA track. "Light of Other Days" opens with a 100% bucolic feel, featuring an enchanting marshmallow flute followed by a devastating pad. The mysterious keyboard draws the listener in; the perfect instrumental that takes you on a journey of no return. "You and the Sun" begins with a jazzy keyboard, followed by a dynamic atmosphere with a prog-metal riff. The vocals of one of the four guests might surprise with their diversity, their distinctiveness, I mean. The mid-track shift evokes "Canterbury" sounds, reminiscent of CARAVAN, with this delicate, understated, soulless yet meticulously crafted variation. "Over the Sleeping Stars" begins with a vibrant bassline and rhythmic percussion on Risto's saxophone. The guitar leads into a fresh, energetic, and catchy instrumental. A festive folk-jazzy vibe at the start, the guitar solo ignites the music; simple, effective, the outro too short to send you soaring into space. "Only One in the Crowd" is a jazz-rock track featuring bass and distinctive keyboards; the vocals add a prog edge. You have to wait for the transitions to truly appreciate the progressive influences, particularly the delicate keyboard solo. The brooding vocals lead into a bluesy guitar solo that we adore, the high notes keeping us on the edge of our seats. This is the album's highlight, showcasing masterful playing. "With a Breath, I Linger" begins with a pastoral flute over a minimalist piano chord. A slow, solemn, almost martial melody, with Hanna and Rafael at the helm, is the perfect way to close this album of concentrated musical notes.Kimmo P'RSTI is the same artist who played in SAMURAI OF PROG, THE GUILDMASTER, and also contributed to Rafael PACHA.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Vitelli has always had a well-stocked address book, including even a few living legends of '70s prog (Anthony Phillips, Tony Pagliuca, and David Cross, to name just a few, have contributed to Ellesmere's previous albums). This even allowed him to bring together no fewer than five exceptional guitarists in 2018 for *From Sea And Beyond* (Alan Benjamin, Trey Gunn, Keith More, Davy O'List, and Brett Kull, no less). On *Stranger Skies*, the lineup of prestigious guests continues. Surrounding the core lineup of Vitelli on bass and keyboards, Giacomo Anselmi (Goblin Rebirth) on electric guitars, Stefano Vicarelli (Fonderia) on Moog and Mellotron, and Mattias Olsson (who needs no introduction)?a master of odd time signatures and off-beat rhythms, who once again brings his crisp, precise, and creative drumming, the band brings together a few musicians?whom, like Olsson, we're tempted to leave unintroduced?including figures from prog of yesterday and today (Clive Nolan, Tomas Bodin, Riccardo Romano), well-known veterans (John Hackett, David Jackson), and others less so, such as Graeme Taylor (one of Gryphon's leaders) or Bob Hodges (Czar).Ellesmere's previous albums were mostly instrumental, featuring occasional guest vocalists (we recall Robert Berry's performance on *From Sea And Beyond*, though perhaps less so that of Luciano Regoli, the leader of Raccomandata Ricevuta Ritorno, an old RPI band) Here, it's the opposite: one and the same voice throughout, that of the remarkable and much-talked-about John Wilkinson. As the lead singer of the Liverpool band The Swan Chorus (with two albums to their credit, one released in 2018 and the other in 2023) and a member of Mama?which, as its name suggests, is a band that covers songs from Genesis's Phil Collins era?John brings a vocal tone so close to Collins's that it's almost uncanny. John Wilkinson can also be heard on a few tracks from the recent Samurai of Prog releases, such as "Like An Endless Sea" from Bernard & P�rsti's *Robinson Crusoe*.With the relative resurgence of the vinyl market offering an opportunity to make a little extra money, some progressive artists don't hesitate to shorten the length of their CDs and organize them into Side A and Side B, with an eye toward a potential vinyl release. Recently, the Canadian band Monarch Trail even titled their new album *Four Sides*, clearly signaling their intention to present it as a double album in the spirit of the golden age of the LP. Similarly, the first four tracks (totaling 23 minutes) of *Stranger Skies* are described as the "cold side" (meaning the more rock-oriented section), and the last two tracks?which are longer (totaling 24 minutes)?as the "hot side" (meaning more progressive). We'll see that it's not quite that simple.At the risk of sounding pedantic, let's dive right in with a track-by-track walkthrough of the album. Track #1, the first on Side A, known as the "cold" side: "Northwards" (6:50). After a majestic introduction in the classical symphonic style featuring Clive Nolan's keyboards, Ellesmere manages to revive?by blending them?the styles that Yes and Genesis had more or less adopted around 1977 (specifically, the tracks "Going For The One" and "Down And Out" as references): a multitrack sound, rich in effects and reverb, and a warm, full-bodied voice saturated with echo. Track #2: "Tundra" (6:43). Closer to early '80s Rush, especially in the chord arpeggios of a martial keyboard and the plump bass line characteristic of the Canadian band (it's no coincidence, by the way, that Vitelli's four-string Fender is named "Geddy Lee"!). A breathtaking fusion guitar solo closes out "Tundra" in the epic style of Dave Bainbridge. Track #3: "Crystallized," the only instrumental. In the intro, performed by Taylor, we catch a glimpse of the "Anthony Philips-style acoustic-pastoral" state of grace from the first album. It's a refreshing and welcome breather amid these intense three-quarters of an hour, with no downtime or let-up?which, paradoxically, might be the only criticism one could level at this album, provided you enjoy symphonic prog with unapologetic grandeur. The next track, a powerful neo-prog piece enhanced by David Jackson's unrestrained saxophone?which adds prog-fusion colors?is more in line with the rest of the album. Track #4: "Arctica" (4:16). The influence of Rush returns, with just as much energy and conviction but without the melodic clarity of the Toronto trio. A slight weak spot on *Stranger Skies*, despite the strength of the performance.Track #5, the first on Side B, known as the "hot" side: "Stranger Skies" (12:17). Closer to Steve Hackett's recent solo albums?his brother is once again on flute here?and less "edgy" than on *Wyrd*. John's vocals naturally seem to draw closer to those of Nad Sylvan. Along the way, one is also reminded of BBT or the most prog-oriented moments of Phil Collins' solo career. Track #6: "Another World" (11:43). We head in the direction of Arena, with Genesis from '78?'80 still in mind, particularly Rutherford's compositions. The final three minutes mark a complete break. Graceful and subtle, exquisite and imaginative, this finale?performed with delicacy by Tomas Bodin, which becomes obvious upon listening?is a lovely coda that stands in stark contrast to everything that came before.With musical themes more captivating than ever, greater cohesion than before, a consistent density that doesn't preclude fluidity, high-quality vocals, and a style a world away from the first album?closer to the subsequent ones while correcting their weaknesses or missteps but retaining their beautiful generosity? *Stranger Skies* is the most captivating of Roberto Vitelli's albums released under the name Ellesmere.

items.body: Review by CeeJayGee — I first discovered The Tangent 15 years ago, but it took me another couple of years to realise how good their music is. For a few years they were one of a handful of bands that I would call my favourites. The quality of the albums over the last few years has been so high that I would now say The Tangent is my favourite and most listened to band. I also appreciate being able to engage with Andie Tillison via social media. After I commented on the quality of this year's Po90 release, aftersometimelater, saying that it deserved to be more heavily marketed to raise its profile, Andie asked me whether I would like to hear some of the forthcoming album, Was. I jumped at the opportunity. I thought I would hear just a couple of tracks but over several weeks I was able to listen to and comment on the entire album. The album tells Andie's story through the music and the events that have shaped his own musical career. You could call it autobiographical. I don't believe anyone has attempted this previously and the purpose of the album has clearly inspired Andie to create some wonderful melodies.The first track I heard was the title track which I found immediately likeable and kept playing on repeat. I loved the simplicity of the riff which develops through the 22 minutes of the track. I couldn't stop playing it after the first listen. I then heard the Was Suite which at over 53 minutes is structured as six named segments that flow perfectly from one to another on the album. In classical music they would be called movements. When I first heard it, it was a single track. This is a largely instrumental piece and my past interest in classical music, and my love of rock and jazz fusion, makes this compulsive listening. The final segment, titled "Let Me Sing", is Andie sharing how he communicates through his music and his messages through poetic lyrics. It is a powerful conclusion which finishes with an inspirational speaker advising a young audience how to have good lives. I then heard Was Not, which Andie indicated to me was his favourite. This is another complex 20 minute plus and certainly matches Was and the Suite in terms of quality. The track opens with Andie's impressions of World War II formed from what he learned from the people who lived through and survived it, and the many films and TV series which his family watched together in his youth. I am a bit older than Andie, but I can empathise with this totally. The track develops with memories of further events and the hope that the World would learn from its past mistakes. He continues that the horrors we all see through the media seem to make us numb and he concludes with a very personal memory of his father in a nursing home. It is an extraordinary piece. The underlying themes and melodies are most enjoyable, but the piece is dominated by the message. For me, these are three standout pieces of music and these tracks are destined to be classics. The album also includes Follow The River plus four bonus tracks (two of which are around 20 minutes long) which are all enjoyable. I have little doubt that this will be my favourite 2026 album and it is likely to end up being my favourite album by The Tangent (so far).

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Logos channels a classic Gothic symphonic rock sound; the use of synthesizers and keyboards in "Origami in SOL" serves as an introduction to a complex musical tapestry reminiscent of Metamorfosi, particularly in "Paesaggi di insonnia," a track that borders on psychedelia through its juxtaposition of keyboard layers. The spirit of Genesis, combined with the saxophone, creates a dense atmosphere that nonetheless flows effortlessly, thanks to a dark, epic jazz influence, driven by a powerful underlying purpose: this is a concept album about the life of Sadako Sasaki. She was a Japanese girl who was two years old at the time of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima; she later fell ill and passed away at the age of twelve. This story gave rise to the Japanese legend of the thousand paper cranes (origami) that Sadako attempted to fold in the hope of recovering.The track's frenetic pace in Un lieto inquietarsi, is comparable to Le Orme's magnum opus, Felona e Sorona; the interplay between the drums, keyboards, and synthesizer weaves a musical tapestry that sets the stage for various solos, while an ominous aura gradually takes hold, including a decidedly non-festive use of the Hammond organ.Shifts in tempo occur naturally, amidst the abruptness with which the music bursts forth, drawing upon the full majesty of the classical repertoire, where Baroque polyphony paves the way for Luca Zerman's vocals, which adapt seamlessly to the context. In Il Sarto one notices the resemblance of Luca Zerman's voice to Aldo Tagliapietra (from Le Orme) and then he is joined by Elisa Montaldo, pianist and singer of the progressive band Il Tempio Delle Clessidre, in a great and emotional duet."Zaini di Elio" begins with the feel of 1970s Genesis, specifically the Phil Collins era, before allowing itself to be captivated by the structures of J.S. Bach; combined with Alessandro Perbellini's drumming, the music takes on the quality of a dance alongside the electric clavichord. It evokes Tony Banks and Phil Collins during the ...And Then There Were Three... period, though the sound drifts toward a more pastoral atmosphere, incorporating traditional vocal elements from the artist's native Verona. The layering of the various keyboard lines is so delicate that the transitions are imperceptible: it sounds as though the music had always been there.Sadako e le mille gru di cartareminds me of Hiroshima Mon Amour, Alain Resnais's film, and the subtlety of addressing such a subject with poetry and respect; stepping back to draw closer from a different angle, the kind of perspective only the passage of time can provide. Here, Claudio Antolini's piano takes on a new depth, and the rhythm that has driven the album pauses. Musical passages evoke Eastern melodies, telling the story through sound, accompanied by ghostly-sounding Minimoog emulations. Never before has a folded sheet, a crumpled scrap of paper, held so many layers of meaning or interpretation. The music provides the accompaniment: dramatic, yet also epic and inspiring, conveying a strength that rises from the ashes. Driven by keyboards and drums, the composition blends classical elements with syncopated rhythms, building toward an operatic finale as the paper figure unfolds, a symbol of the hope that nothing happens in vain, even if it seems otherwise at the time. That was precisely the hidden meaning behind the twists and intersections of the music itself.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — For the most part early 70s German Krautrock morphed into the more instrumentally demanding Krautjazz fusion that found a rather sizable following in the second half of the decade when prog ingeneral had declined. Some bands though found a nice middle ground between the heady koschmischevibes of the space age and placed them alongside the more focused workouts of the jazz fusion scene.One such band was MORPHEUS that was spawned from an earlier band called Opossum which existed from1971 to 1975 but was never successful at releasing its own material although an archival releasewould see the light of day decades later in 2003. While Opossum was a more free form jazz kinda Kraut, a couple members wanted to play more psych-soaked structured tracks in the vein of other German fusion acts such as Kraan and Missus Beastleyor Embryo for that matter. The results was the short-lived MORPHEUS from Warburg that existed fortwo years from 1975 to 1977 and released its one and only album RABENTEUER smack dab in the middleof its career in 1976. Far from free form, MORPHEUS gathered grooves from the world of prog rock,trippy effects from the Kraut scene and more accessible jazz stylings also from the German scene.The result was a nicely displayed album that rocked, was smothered in jazz and offered a moresubdued heady vibe courtesy of spacey effects and a sensual flautist on board.Another of the many rarities that were generated during the era, RABENTEUER was limited to 500copies and went undiscovered until the Garden of Delights label resurrected the album for a 1998 CDrelease. Steeped in psych-fueled jazz rock, RABENTEUER features six all-instrumental tracks thatoffer funk-fueled bass grooves, gnarled workouts that offer labyrinthine structured compositions toflow around a rather accessible compositional flair only fortified with complex soundscapes,bountiful helpings of time signature deviations and ample doses of soloing between the variousmusicians that consisted of Peter Bl�meke (bass, flute), Gerold Adler (guitar), Heinrich Holtgreve(alto saxophone) and Alfred Franke (drums). While the tracks are primarily upbeat and more in thejazz rock camp, "Tanz Der Morphine" takes a dive into the space rock world of koschmische Kraut.Like many of the similarly minded bands of the era, MORPHEUS delivered the chops as far as jazz-infused prog was concerned with nice accessible hooks augmented by the more complex attributes ofthe words of both prog and fusion however the album as competently performed as it is sounds a bitlike those same similarly minded acts that didn't really add a lot to the world of jazz fusion atthis stage in the game. The tracks are pleasant but almost by the books in approach without any realfiery passion emerging by the rather consistent display of instrumental interplay. Overall it's anice supplemental piece from the era but not one that strikes me as utterly essential either.Pleasant but not much else. The CD version offers an extra long 20-minute jam track but this is evenof less interest than the album in general.3.5 rounded down

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the many one and done acts that emerged in Germany's fertile Krautrock scene actually lastedfrom 1973 when it formed in Bottrop until the band folded in 1980. While only releasing one album,1975's BROKEN DOOR, the band went through many lineup changes with only one version of the bandmanaging to record and release something but even though a single album was recorded and set tovinyl, it was produced in such low numbers that it was virtually forgotten shortly after its releasealthough the band did frequent the live circuits for its entire run. Luckily BROKEN DOOR was rescuedby the Garden of Delights label and has emerged as one of those unexpected gems that was almostcompletely lost to history.With a rather contradictory band name juxtaposed to a disheartening album title, PROSPER wassomewhat unique and whereas some German prog was not Krautrock and not all Krautrock wasprogressive, PROSPER found the nice in-between zone that allowed the headier atmospheric texturesand spaciness of the koschmische sounds exist in full space rock mode all the while offering anabundance of virtuosic instrumental moments mostly courtesy of guitarist Evert Brettschneider whowas concurrently active in the jazz fusion group Contract Trio. Not surprisingly some of thisjazziness seeped into PROSPER which works surprisingly well. Add some King Crimson grit to the mixand you're in for a real treat with this one.The album is primarily instrumental dishing out a multitude of space rock-tinged motifs laced withmoments of progressive rock heft and jazzy accouterments. The band was a five-piece but implementeda diverse array of guitar tones (both acoustic and electric) as well as a plethora of keys rangingfrom the Fender Rhodes and Mini-Moog to mellotrons and other electronic effects however the thumpingbass grooves clearly point to Amon Dull II's heady mix of kosmische kraftiness. The album featuredeight tracks which range from softer contemplative space rock to more jazz-fueled prog. The opening"Beginning" offers a nice rotisserie of all the styles on the menu and elegantly passes the batonfrom one genre shift to another. The band's dexterity in handling the instrumentation allows thealbum to take on a more epic feel as opposed to many Kraut acts that were simply going for theescapist approach.While the album is fairly uniform in its feel, the mid-album clunker "Your Country" sounds woefullyout of place with its country rock style that wouldn't have sounded out of place on an album fromThe Band and although competently performed somewhat derails the momentum of the album's continuityhowever the surrounding material is strong enough to allow the listener to merely shrug it off assome kind of unfortunate anomaly. Overall PROSPER's debut release is indeed a true gem that took thebest aspects of the varying Krautrock and prog styles of the era and seamlessly agglutinated it allinto a cohesive sound of its own right. This is indeed a band that should've released another albumor two before evaporating into the 1980s but like many bands of the day, we're actually lucky toeven have the opportunity to experience this one once rare and unknown band's sole artifact.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — Sometimes a rest is as good as a change. Having disbanded after the underwhelming "Lantaloon", DANDO SHAFT resurfaced for one 1977 album with all the principals still available, though Polly doesn't sing any lead at all and is almost just there for the credits. In the meantime, a few dignitaries help expand the credit list, namely ROD CLEMENTS of LINDISFARNE and DANNY THOMPSON of PENTANGLE both on bass, as well as a fledgling saxophonist Paul Dunmall who usurps the spotlight whether it's on him or not. But is it prog? And is it good? Yes. It's that rare comeback album from the late 1970s that pleasantly surprises. It asks the "what if" question or makes the "if only" statement , in this case, could this have changed the bands fortunes if released in 1973? The rock component, notably the bluesy electric guitars and percussions, are just one aspect that elevates this above DANDO's usual twee personae, with the violins fitting like a fiddle, illuminating the mastery of "Follow You", perhaps the group's best track, and "Feel Like I wanna go home". "Trees" marks the return of the olde Englishe and Celtic credentials, even more formidably on the sophisticated "Lady and Man", If it weren't for the preponderance of average albeit absolutely competent numbers, I could give this a roundup, but it's still a miniature triumph worthy of highness if not majesty.
